record.original_question: Construct a convincing computer visualization of the Julia set of a Cremer polynomial f_lambda(z) = lambda z + z^2, where theta is irrational and the map is not analytically conjugate to a rotation near 0.

evidence.quote: Let fλ(z) = λz + z 2 where λ = exp(2πiθ). Call such a polynomial parabolic if θ is rational. If θ is irrational, and fλ is analytically conjugate to a rotation near 0 we say fλ is a Siegel polynomial. Otherwise we call fλ a Cremer polynomial.
Question 3. Make a good computer picture of the Julia set of some Cremer polynomial.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For $\lambda = e^{2\pi i \theta}$ with $\theta \in \mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, consider the quadratic polynomial
$$f_\lambda(z) = \lambda z + z^2,$$
which fixes $0$ with multiplier $\lambda$. The map $f_\lambda$ is called a Siegel polynomial if it is analytically conjugate, in some neighborhood of $0$, to the rigid rotation $z \mapsto \lambda z$; otherwise (still with $\theta$ irrational) it is called a Cremer polynomial. Recall that the (filled) Julia set of $f_\lambda$ is the set of points whose forward orbit under iteration of $f_\lambda$ is bounded, and its Julia set $J(f_\lambda)$ is the topological boundary of this set.

Produce a convincing, mathematically faithful computer-generated picture of the Julia set $J(f_\lambda)$ for some choice of irrational $\theta$ for which $f_\lambda$ is a Cremer polynomial. Equivalently, exhibit an effective algorithm which, given a precision $\varepsilon > 0$, outputs an image approximating $J(f_\lambda)$ in the Hausdorff metric to within $\varepsilon$, together with the resulting picture.
artifact.status_search_result: Significant progress has been made but the problem in its strongest form is not fully resolved. Braverman and Yampolsky proved that there exist computable irrational rotation numbers $\theta$ for which the Cremer Julia set $J(f_\lambda)$ is not computable, i.e., no algorithm can produce arbitrarily accurate pictures — a strong obstruction to "convincing visualization" in general. Conversely, for certain restricted classes of Cremer rotation numbers, computable approximations and partial visualizations have been achieved (work of Binder, Braverman, Yampolsky and others on computational complexity of Cremer Julia sets). Thus the question is partially solved: some Cremer Julia sets are provably non-visualizable, while others can be drawn with rigorous guarantees.

status_evidence.title: Constructing Non-Computable Julia Sets
status_evidence.snippet: It is possible to constructively produce examples of quadratic polynomials, whose Julia sets are not computable.
status_evidence.claim: Some Cremer Julia sets are provably non-computable, so no algorithm can draw them to arbitrary precision.

status_evidence.title: On computational complexity of Cremer Julia sets
status_evidence.snippet: Computational complexity of Cremer Julia sets is studied, with both computability and non-computability results depending on the rotation number.
status_evidence.claim: Computability and complexity of drawing Cremer Julia sets depend on arithmetic properties of theta; some are computable, others are not.

status_evidence.title: Computability of Julia Sets (Braverman–Yampolsky)
status_evidence.snippet: Monograph covering computability and non-computability of Julia sets including Cremer cases.
status_evidence.claim: The visualization question has been addressed via the framework of computability of Julia sets, yielding partial positive and negative answers.
